Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa took the church's property and its independence, and was only completed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession.

Christian III won a civil war, arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and the church ordinance drawn up with Luther's colleague Johannes Bugenhagen reorganized the churches of Denmark, Norway and Iceland at a stroke.
Icelandic resistance ended in 1550 with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop.

These became the Lutheran churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland — still the largest churches in their countries, and in several cases still formally established or closely tied to the state.

Caught between the Ottoman and Safavid empires, Armenians lived through one of the great forced migrations of their history: in 1604-05 Shah Abbas I, pursuing a scorched-earth strategy against the Ottomans, deported the population of Julfa and much of eastern Armenia into Persia, and many died on the road.
